extracted.intended_audience: British legislators, statesmen, and the politically engaged public considering constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for designing and evaluating a national constitution and its institutions (representation, executive, local government, monetary policy) with attention to human nature, continuity, and coherence. Focused on pitfalls of abstract, arithmetical schemes and the practical requirements for durable republican government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution must form one consistent whole and not be a patchwork of contradictory principles reluctantly held together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid combining several conflicting metaphysical or mathematical schemes; multiple contradictory principles will claw and bite each other to mutual destruction. A constitution should not be several incompatible systems forced into one frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to moral and political concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution should expressly engage with moral and political matters—the actions, passions, and interests of men—not only abstract metaphysics or arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is remarkable when arrangements of mankind contain 'not one reference whatsoever' to moral or political concerns; founders must consider moral and civic conditions, not only abstract principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of human nature and civil habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators must study human nature and the secondary effects of civil habits produced by education, profession, residence, and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good legislators examine how birth, education, profession, life-period, town/country residence, methods of acquiring property, and the quality of property create different 'species' of citizens and shape appropriate institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of citizens and appropriate allotment of privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens should be classed according to their differing habits and aptitudes and assigned roles or privileges suited to those distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient republican legislators apportioned citizens into classes and appropriated privileges to secure each description what its occasions required; modern schemes that reduce all men to a homogeneous mass risk removing protections and force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid severing the nation into independent republics
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't design a constitution that divides the country into many practically independent republics without constitutional means of coherence or subordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partitioning into cantons/communes/departments with no central, standing authority tends to dissociate the nation and prevent effective unity, leaving only acquiescence as the tenuous bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a standing, fundamental government (trustee for the whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a standing, unalterable fundamental government to which local representations and districts are subordinate and from which their representation originates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central government acts as the point of reference and trustee for the whole (as in the King and House of Lords), securing equality among districts and giving the representative system coherence; without it, representation is fragmented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct accountability of representatives (avoid excessive intermediary elections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Electoral design should preserve a clear link between constituent electors and their representatives; multi-stage elections that interpose several bodies sever responsibility and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three-tier election schemes produce 'ambassadors of a state' not 'representatives of the people'; when two sets of magistracy intervene, the representative is too remote to be called to account by primary electors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electorate's ability to judge fitness and retain influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections must provide means for electors to know a candidate's fitness and to retain some hold on him by personal obligation or dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal choice is especially unfit for long chains of delegation: if primary electors cannot know qualities of the representative and cannot hold him accountable, election fails its real purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and experience in representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow continuity of service so representatives can learn and exercise their functions effectively; avoid arbitrary ineligibilities that remove experienced legislators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules that make former legislators ineligible for periods (e.g., two years) just as they learn their trade produce superficial, interrupted, and ill-informed governance ('their bottoms are supposed foul').

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide an intermediate revising body (senate or council)
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic requires some senate-like body or council to provide steadiness, consistency, and a point of contact for foreign states and the people between the supreme assembly and the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No purely single active assembly with executive officers can substitute for this middle place; its absence is a sovereign incapacity and undermines long-term moderation and deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive with deliberative discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive must not be merely a passive machine or channel to the legislature; it should possess some deliberative discretion and meaningful role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'degraded king' made only a conduit to the Assembly renders the executive impotent and yet makes the legislative omnipotent and unbalanced; meaningful executive function is necessary for governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on confiscation and forced paper currency as constitutional cement
rubrics_metrics.description: Using confiscation of property together with compulsory paper currency to bind the state is an unstable and dangerous means of cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If confiscation cannot sustain paper money (as likely), these measures will increase dissociation and confusion; their success would undermine the very cement when the paper sinks, making cohesion precarious and contingent on credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary stability and protection of economic incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: A stable medium of exchange and predictability of value are essential; forcing speculative paper instruments into daily life destroys industry, economy, and prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When money fluctuates wildly, industry and economy suffer: 'Who will labor without knowing the amount of his pay?' Paper assignats of varying value will destroy economy, saving, and care, turning a nation into speculators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of financial power in managers and speculators
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary schemes that substitute paper for real money and enable managers to transmute land and paper centralize power in the hands of money directors and speculators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A forced paper circulation and sale of confiscated lands empowers managers to control revenue and a large fraction of land, creating an oligarchy of money-jobbers and speculators who dominate the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect local knowledge and habits in appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Local magistrates, revenue collectors, bishops, and curates should be acquainted with their districts and possess habitual civic connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New officials detached from local civil habitude produce ineffective administration; local knowledge and longstanding relations are the 'soul of a true republic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing political unity on abstract geometrical/arithmetic division
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on geometrical distribution or arithmetical equality (equal-sized squares, etc.) as the basis for political identity or attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People's attachments arise from family, neighborhood, habit, and provincial connections, not from belonging to a numbered square; artificial equalization will not produce genuine public affection or durable unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require substantive constitutional means of coherence beyond ceremonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating festivals, spectacles, and civic feasts as primary means of binding the state; real constitutional mechanisms are needed for coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confederations and spectacles are 'mere tricks' and will not substitute for institutions and structures that genuinely bind disparate parts of a nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance social orders to guard against despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper classification and distribution of power among different orders and classes act as barriers against the excesses of despotism and are necessary for a durable republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient legislators' division of citizens into orders was key to protecting liberty; levelling all orders removes indirect restraints that mitigate despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent ephemeral, unorganized local leadership from being overpowered
rubrics_metrics.description: Design must account for how country (rural) populations lack the combination and incorporation habits of towns and so are vulnerable to being economically and politically dominated by urban moneyed interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Town combination and money influence advantage urban directors; without institutional protections, landed gentry and peasants cannot sustain influence or protect property from market manipulations by speculators.
